Richland County by the numbers

Where is Richland County and what is in it?

Richland County is in the Midlands of South Carolina, and its seat is Columbia, which is also the state capital and the largest community. The county covers 771.96 square miles, with 757.28 of land and 14.68 of water.

Besides Columbia, the municipalities are Cayce, Forest Acres, Arcadia Lakes, Blythewood, Eastover, Elgin and Irmo.

  • Fairfield and Newberry counties lie to the north and northwest.
  • Kershaw and Sumter counties are to the northeast and east.
  • Lexington County is to the west and Calhoun County to the south.

The county's 2020 Census population was 416,147.

What is the history of Richland County?

Richland County was established on March 12, 1785, and is probably named for its rich land. It began as part of the Camden District, and its boundaries were formally incorporated on December 18, 1799.

Landmarks that define it today include the South Carolina State House in downtown Columbia, the University of South Carolina, Fort Jackson and the McEntire Joint National Guard Base. Riverbanks Zoo is reached by I-126.

Parcels in Eastover, Blythewood, Irmo or Columbia all pay through the same county Treasurer at 2020 Hampton Street.

What drives the Richland County economy?

Health care and social assistance is the largest employment sector in Richland County, at 15.3% of jobs in the third quarter of 2023. Prisma Health was the largest employer in 2019 with 16,000 employees.

Output in 2022 was about $32 billion, or roughly $75,222 per person.

Where do you pay Richland County property tax?

Richland County property tax is paid through the Treasurer at 2020 Hampton Street, Columbia, SC 29204, open Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. The main number is 803-576-2250.

Taxes can be paid online, in person or by mail, and the county offers a monthly payment plan. The Treasurer's pages list separate emails for customer service (treasurer@richlandcountysc.gov), planned payments and tax sale questions.

  • State law makes January 15 the end of the penalty-free window (S.C. Code 12-45-70).
  • A 3% penalty follows, then 7% more before February 2 and 5% more before March 17 (S.C. Code 12-45-180).
  • A payment plan does not stop further action unless the full amount is paid.

Statute section 12-45-180 also waives penalties when title transferred during the tax year and the new owner never received a timely notice.

What does the Richland County tax sale look like?

Richland County's tax sale is typically held each fall and is run as a sealed bid auction, and the 2026 sale was set for November 2 and 3 at the Richland County Township Auditorium, 1703 Taylor Street, Columbia. Property is sold as is, for cash, to the highest bidder.

To stop a property from being sold, the Treasurer's office had to receive payment by 5 p.m. on Friday, October 30, 2026, in cash or certified cashier's check. Personal, company and escrow checks were not accepted.

  • Bidders register online only, and the fee is $50.00.
  • The opening bid is the delinquent taxes, sale costs and current year taxes.
  • A winning bidder who does not pay owes $500 per bid plus court costs.
  • Buyers receive title without warranty, and the county can cancel a sale before a deed is issued.

Dates change each year, so ask the Treasurer for the next schedule. The pages we read do not state the redemption period or interest rates, so ask the office for those as well.

How often does Richland County reassess?

The Richland County Assessor conducts a countywide reassessment every five years, consistent with S.C. Code 12-43-217. The Assessor's page does not name the next year, so ask the office at 803-576-2640.

The state rule also says taxpayers must be notified when value or classification changes by $1,000 or more. A county can delay putting new values into effect by ordinance for no more than one tax year.

The Assessor's office also handles rollback taxes on farmland that changes use, HOA properties, active military residential exemptions and deed sale records. The office also lists multiple-lot and builder or developer discounts, commercial ATI exemptions and mailing address changes among its services, so tell it when you sell or move.

How do you appeal a Richland County assessment?

File a written objection with the Assessor within 90 days of the dated reassessment notice, or by the first penalty date on the tax bill if no notice was sent. For online appeals, the deadline is whichever comes first.

  1. File through the county's "Appeal Your Assessment" portal or in writing.
  2. Attach documents that dispute the assessed value or classification.
  3. If a representative files for you, submit a power of attorney on SC DOR Form SC2848.
  4. For an LLC or similar owner, include Articles of Organization or an Operating Agreement.

The Assessor is at 2020 Hampton Street, Suite 2058, Columbia, SC 29204, with a mailing address of P.O. Box 192, Columbia, SC 29202. The phone is 803-576-2640 and the email is assessoroffice@richlandcountysc.gov. The county site also lists a Board of Assessment Appeals that hears disputes between the Assessor and the taxpayer.

What does the 4% legal residence rate mean in Richland County?

Qualifying owner-occupied homes move from the 6% assessment ratio to 4% once residency and ownership requirements are met. State law covers the home plus up to five contiguous acres, and the owner may not rent it for more than 72 days in a calendar year (S.C. Code 12-43-220).

If an owner loses eligibility and fails to report it within six months, the statute allows a penalty of 100% of the tax paid plus interest of 0.5% per month, with a $30 minimum.

Landlords and heirs who do not live in the house should expect the 6% rate. Active-duty residents with South Carolina duty stations are treated as domiciled here under the same section.

What do Richland County sellers usually face?

Sellers in Richland County often hold an inherited house, a rental with a tax bill in arrears, or a home in poor condition.

  • Treasurer, 803-576-2250: current bill and tax sale questions.
  • Assessor, 803-576-2640: rate, value and appeals.
  • Deed recording: $1.85 per $500 of value, split $1.30 state and $0.55 county (S.C. Code 12-24-10), with deeds in lieu of foreclosure exempt.

Cash Home Buyers buys houses in their current condition, so a seller with an older house can request an offer without making repairs. Get a payoff number from the Treasurer first so you know what must come out of the proceeds.

January 15 is the last day to pay without penalty under state law. A 3% penalty applies afterward.

Where is the Richland County Treasurer?

It is at 2020 Hampton Street, Columbia, SC 29204, open 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday to Friday. The phone is 803-576-2250.

How do I appeal my Richland County assessment?

File a written objection with the Assessor within 90 days of the reassessment notice. The county has an online appeal portal, and a representative needs Form SC2848.

Does Richland County have payment plans for property tax?

Yes, the Treasurer offers a monthly payment plan, but the full amount must be paid to avoid further action.

When is the Richland County tax sale?

It is typically held each fall. The 2026 sale was set for November 2 and 3 at 1703 Taylor Street in Columbia.

How do I contact the Richland County Assessor?

Call 803-576-2640 or email assessoroffice@richlandcountysc.gov. The office is at 2020 Hampton Street, Suite 2058, Columbia, and is open 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday to Friday.

What proof does an LLC need to appeal a Richland County assessment?

An LLC or other non-natural owner must provide its Articles of Organization or Operating Agreement. A power of attorney is also needed if the representative is not a member of the entity.

Can I sell a Richland County house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. The tax is paid from the proceeds at closing, and Cash Home Buyers can buy the house as it is.

Greenville County by the numbers

Where is Greenville County and how is it laid out?

Greenville County sits in the northwest corner of South Carolina's Upstate, against the North Carolina line. It covers 795.57 square miles, of which 785.93 are land, and the city of Greenville is both the county seat and its largest community.

The northern boundary follows the crest of the Blue Ridge Mountains, so the county reaches higher country than most of the state. The 2010 Census lists six cities: Fountain Inn, Greenville, Greer, Mauldin, Simpsonville and Travelers Rest. Fountain Inn and Greer each spill across a county line, into Laurens and Spartanburg counties.

Much of the population lives in places that are not cities at all. Taylors, Berea, Wade Hampton, Five Forks, Gantt and Slater-Marietta are census-designated places, and each has its own mix of older ranch homes, newer subdivisions and mill-era cottages.

For a seller this layout matters because a house in Travelers Rest near the mountains and a house in Mauldin near the interstate are taxed by the same county offices but sell to very different buyers.

What is the history behind Greenville County?

The state legislature created Greenville County in 1786, and the name honors General Nathanael Greene, the Revolutionary War commander of the southern campaign. The early spelling was "Greeneville."

The county grew out of the old Ninety-Six District as settlers moved into the backcountry. The census count was 6,503 in 1790 and 53,490 in 1900. By 1950 it had reached 168,152, and it has kept climbing since.

That long growth curve explains why a single county can hold homes from the 1900s, the mill villages, the postwar subdivisions and houses finished last year. Age is the first thing a cash buyer looks at when estimating repairs, and Greenville County has every age.

How big is Greenville County and what does its economy rely on?

Greenville County is the most populous county in South Carolina, with 525,534 residents in the 2020 Census and a 2025 estimate of 583,125. Its 2022 economic output was about $40.6 billion, and unemployment ran between 2.1 and 3.3 percent from 2022 to 2024.

Health care and social assistance is the largest industry by jobs, with 43,180 workers out of 292,366. Manufacturing follows with 31,693 jobs, then retail trade with 30,485.

  • Employers named for the county include Bon Secours, Charter Communications, GE Vernova, Lockheed Martin and Michelin.
  • Prisma Health, Publix, TD Bank, the Postal Service and Walmart appear on the same list.
  • These sectors are the county's biggest sources of paychecks.

The 2025 estimate shows the county still adding people.

What roads, airports and rail serve Greenville County?

Interstates 85, 185 and 385 are the main highways, with US 25, 29, 123 and 276 crossing the county as well. Many residents live along these corridors and drive to jobs elsewhere in the county.

Greenville-Spartanburg International Airport lies mostly in Spartanburg County, while Donaldson Center Airport and Greenville Downtown Airport are inside Greenville County. Amtrak serves the city at its Greenville station.

A cash buyer prices location in whatever it is, so you do not have to stage the house or wait for a buyer who likes the road.

When are Greenville County property taxes due, and what does a late bill cost?

Real property tax in Greenville County is due without penalty by January 15. Bills usually go out near the end of October, according to the county's Real Property Services calendar.

DateWhat is added
January 15Last day to pay with no penalty
January 163 percent
February 2Further 7 percent
March 17Further 5 percent plus a $15.00 execution cost

These dates match S.C. Code 12-45-180. The Tax Collector says penalties come off only when there is direct evidence of a county error.

The office is in the South Building, Suite 1100-S, and the phone is 864.467.7050. You can pay in person, by mail or online, and most payments post within three to five business days.

The county also states that the tax on a property follows the property, not the person. If you sell with the current year unpaid, the title company normally settles the balance from your proceeds.

How does selling a house change the assessment in Greenville County?

A sale is usually an assessable transfer of interest, which means the county revalues the house to a current date. Real Property Services says the 15 percent cap on increases is removed after such a transfer, and a point-of-sale reassessment uses a December 31 appraisal date for the year of the transfer.

Ownership on January 1 decides whose name is printed on the bill. If the deed changes after that date, both the old and new owners appear on that year's bill, and only the new owner appears the following year. A new assessment notice usually arrives the year after the change.

  • Owner-occupied homes get the 4 percent legal residence assessment, plus a credit that removes the school operating tax. The application must be hand-delivered or postmarked by January 15 with an original signature, and electronic filing is not accepted.
  • A buyer who will not live in the house loses that treatment, so the bill can rise sharply for the next owner.
  • The county lists a January 30 deadline for the 25 percent exemption on transfers made the previous year.

Telling your buyer about this ahead of time avoids a surprise after closing. A short call to Real Property Services at 864.467.7300 clears up anything unclear.

How do you appeal a Greenville County assessment?

You appeal in writing, and the first deadline is printed on your assessment notice. If no notice was sent, the usual deadline is January 15, or the next working day if that falls on a weekend or holiday.

The statute behind this is S.C. Code 12-60-2510, which gives 90 days from the mailing of a notice that raised value by $1,000 or more.

  1. Mail a written objection with the tax map number, your reasons and your opinion of value. Email and fax are not accepted, and the postmark decides timeliness.
  2. A certified appraiser reviews every timely appeal, and the assessor mails the result.
  3. You have 30 days from the notice of decision to protest to the County Board of Assessment Appeals.
  4. You have 30 days after the Board's written decision to go to the Administrative Law Judge Division.

Appeals go to Real Property Services at Greenville County Square, Suite 1000. The office schedules notices for new construction and other increases in late summer or early fall.

What happens if Greenville County taxes go unpaid?

After March 17 the bill is delinquent and the Tax Collector issues an execution notice. If the bill is still unpaid 30 days after that notice is mailed, a Notice of Seizure follows by certified mail with restricted delivery.

The sale is a public auction at the Greenville Convention Center on Exposition Drive. The sale is advertised once a week for three weeks first, and the opening bid covers all delinquent tax, penalties and costs plus the current year's tax.

The owner, a grantee, or a mortgage or judgment creditor can redeem within 12 months. Interest on the bid is 3 percent in months one to three, 6 percent in months four to six, 9 percent in months seven to nine and 12 percent in months ten to twelve. If nobody redeems, the buyer gets a tax deed that conveys only the county's interest, not a warranty deed.

Selling before the auction is often cleaner than letting the process run. A sale closes the debt through escrow, and you avoid the redemption interest.

What does it cost to record the deed in Greenville County?

Deeds are recorded at the Register of Deeds in Suite S-2100 of Greenville County Square, 301 University Ridge, Monday to Friday from 8:30 am to 5:00 pm. The office asks you to arrive by 4:30 pm.

The state deed recording fee is $1.85 for each $500 of value or part of it, according to S.C. Code Title 12, Chapter 24. The statute splits that into $1.30 for the state and $0.55 for the county. Some transfers are exempt, including a deed in lieu of foreclosure to the mortgagee and certain family partnership or trust transfers.

Your title or escrow company normally prepares the deed and pays the fee from closing funds. If you mail a deed yourself, include a cover letter with a phone number, a stamped return envelope and a check payable to Greenville County.

More questions about Greenville County, SC Property Tax Guide

When are Greenville County property taxes due?

Greenville County real property tax is due without penalty by January 15. A 3 percent penalty starts January 16, another 7 percent on February 2, and another 5 percent plus a $15.00 execution cost on March 17.

Can I sell my Greenville County house if the taxes are unpaid?

Yes. Unpaid tax follows the property, so it is paid from your sale proceeds at closing. A cash purchase can close with the balance cleared through escrow.

Who handles assessment appeals in Greenville County?

Real Property Services does, at Greenville County Square, Suite 1000, phone 864.467.7300. Objections must be in writing, and the postmark decides whether you met the deadline.

Does selling my home raise the next owner's tax bill?

Often it does. A sale is usually an assessable transfer of interest, which removes the 15 percent cap and sets a new value. The buyer also loses the 4 percent legal residence rate if the house is not their home.

How long do I have to redeem a house sold at a Greenville County tax sale?

You have 12 months from the sale. The owner, a grantee, or a mortgage or judgment creditor can redeem by paying the taxes, penalties, costs and the stepped interest on the bid.

Lexington County by the numbers

Where is Lexington County and what does it include?

Lexington County is in the Midlands of South Carolina and is part of the Columbia metropolitan area. It covers 757.62 square miles, with 58.62 of those square miles being water, mostly because of Lake Murray.

The town of Lexington is the county seat and largest community, with 23,568 residents in 2020. West Columbia, Cayce, Irmo, Batesburg-Leesville, Chapin and Gaston are among the other municipalities, and large unincorporated places include Seven Oaks, Oak Grove, Red Bank and White Knoll. Parts of Columbia, Cayce, Irmo and Batesburg-Leesville cross county lines into Richland or Saluda counties.

Neighbors are Richland, Orangeburg, Calhoun, Aiken, Saluda and Newberry counties. Development has concentrated in the eastern and northeastern parts, which is the side nearest Columbia. A lake-area house, a subdivision near Irmo and a rural parcel near Gilbert are all in one county, but they sell on very different timelines.

How fast has Lexington County grown?

Lexington County grew from 262,391 residents in 2010 to 293,991 in the 2020 census, an increase of 12.0 percent. Its estimate for 2025 is 317,588, which makes it the sixth most populous county in the state.

The county was chartered in 1785 and named for Lexington, Massachusetts. About 74.8 percent of residents lived in urban areas in 2020. Rapid growth tends to raise assessed values at the next reassessment, so a seller who bought several years ago may see a bigger tax bill than the one they planned around.

What drives the Lexington County economy?

Health care, retail and food service lead Lexington County employment, and the county's 2022 gross domestic product was $16.7 billion. In the third quarter of 2023 health care and social assistance supplied 14.9 percent of jobs, retail 13.9 percent and accommodation and food services 9.9 percent.

The employers listed for 2021 were:

  • Lexington Medical Center, 7,893 employees
  • Lexington School District 1, 3,674
  • Amazon, 3,050
  • Walmart, 2,603
  • State government, 2,308
  • Michelin, 2,240
  • County of Lexington, 1,855

Distribution centers cluster in the Saxe Gotha Industrial Park near Cayce. A mix of hospital, school and state jobs means sellers here are not tied to one employer, though a house with a leaking roof still needs repair or a buyer who will take it as is.

What roads, schools and weather should a Lexington County seller know about?

Three interstates touch Lexington County: I-20, I-26 and I-77, which begins in Cayce. Columbia Metropolitan Airport serves the area and the COMET authority provides public transit.

Five school districts cover parts of the county, and District 1 is the largest, with 27,072 students and 31 schools. Midlands Technical College and the county library system are also based here.

The climate is humid. Average rainfall is about 47 inches a year, with a July high near 92 degrees and a January low near 33 degrees. Wet summers are hard on roofs, gutters and crawl spaces, and a house on or near Lake Murray or the Saluda, Broad and Congaree rivers should be checked for drainage and flood questions before a buyer's inspector does it.

Who do you contact about Lexington County property tax?

The Treasurer collects, the Assessor values the property and the Auditor handles exemptions. All three are county offices with their own numbers:

  • Treasurer: 212 South Lake Drive, Suite 101, Lexington, SC 29072; (803) 785-8217; open Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
  • Delinquent Tax Department: (803) 785-8345
  • Tax Assessor: (803) 785-8190, for exemptions, sales, address changes, appraisals and rollback taxes
  • Auditor: (803) 785-8181, for homestead exemptions and refunds

Payments can be made in person, online at lex-co.sc.gov, by mailed check to PO Box 604397, Charlotte, NC 28260-4397, or through the night deposit box in front of the County Administration Building. Card payments carry convenience fees, and the postmark decides whether a mailed check is late.

When are Lexington County property taxes due?

Lexington County real property notices are mailed to the owner of record after October 1, and full payment is due by January 15 of the next year. Payments postmarked after that date pick up penalties on January 16, February 2 and March 17.

The Treasurer's page does not give the percentages, but S.C. Code 12-45-180 sets them at 3 percent, then an added 7 percent, then an added 5 percent. Penalties keep accruing during a penalty appeal unless the full amount is paid, and the county refunds penalties already paid if the appeal is granted. The Treasurer takes written penalty appeals; call (803) 785-8217 for instructions.

The county also runs an installment program for real property that is not paid through escrow. Enrollees make five advance payments based on the prior year's tax, and the balance is billed by November 15. Enrollment renews each year, and opting out requires written consent, so a seller in the program should ask the Treasurer how to handle it before closing.

How do you appeal a Lexington County assessment?

A Lexington County owner files a written appeal with the Assessor within 90 days of the date on the assessment notice. If no notice arrived, the county's FAQ says the window is January 1 through January 15 of the following year.

The county reviews appeals on market value, and disagreeing with the dollar amount of the bill is not a ground. If the appeal is not resolved by December 31, the bill is based on at least 80 percent of the assessed value, and tax is still due January 15. After resolution, you either get a refund with interest or owe the difference with interest.

The county has a nine-member Board of Assessment Appeals appointed by County Council. It meets when requested in the Council Chambers of the County Administration Building, and its agendas are posted on the county meeting portal. The state notice rule applies as well: notices are required when value rises $1,000 or more, and the county page says the previous reassessments were in 2015 and 2020 on a five-year cycle, so ask the Assessor for the current schedule.

What changes when a Lexington County house is sold?

The seller's unpaid tax is settled from the proceeds at closing, and the buyer must apply for the 4 percent legal residence ratio. State law says that application must be filed before the first penalty date of the year the owner first claims it.

Common seller problems in Lexington County include:

  • A rental house that fails the 72-day limit and carries the 6 percent ratio.
  • Installment enrollment that nobody canceled after a sale.
  • A bill sent to an old address because the Assessor was never told about a move.
  • A lake or older neighborhood house needing a roof, septic or foundation work before a lender will approve a buyer.

If the tax is behind and repairs are the obstacle, an as-is cash sale lets the title company pay the county out of proceeds. The Delinquent Tax Department at (803) 785-8345 can give you the payoff, and the Treasurer's page does not describe tax sale dates, so ask that office directly.

More questions about Lexington County, SC Property Tax Guide

What is the Lexington County property tax due date?

Full payment is due by January 15 of the year after the tax year, per the county Treasurer. Penalties begin on January 16.

Where is the Lexington County Treasurer's office?

It is at 212 South Lake Drive, Suite 101, Lexington, SC 29072. The phone is (803) 785-8217 and hours are Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

How long do I have to appeal a Lexington County assessment?

You have 90 days from the date on the assessment notice. If you never received one, the county says to appeal between January 1 and January 15 of the following year.

Does Lexington County have an installment plan?

Yes, for real property not paid through escrow. You make five advance payments based on last year's tax, and the balance is billed by November 15.

Can I mail my Lexington County tax payment?

Yes, by check only, to PO Box 604397, Charlotte, NC 28260-4397. The U.S. postmark decides whether it is late.

Can I sell a Lexington County house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. The title company pays the balance from the sale proceeds at closing. Call the Delinquent Tax Department at (803) 785-8345 for the current amount.

Horry County was created from Georgetown District in 1801, when its estimated population was 550. It is named for Revolutionary War hero Peter Horry.

Rivers and swamps isolated residents for generations, and they called the place "The Independent Republic of Horry." Even in 1950 the county had only 59,820 people.

How does flooding affect Horry County houses?

Flooding is a major concern in Horry County because the Waccamaw and Pee Dee rivers and the Intracoastal Waterway all run through it, and water covers about 9 percent of the county. The county's flood resilience plan says Hurricane Florence damaged more than 2,000 buildings in Horry County and closed more than 460 roads.

Florence was the third major riverine flood in four years, after Matthew and Joaquin. Bucksport, Longs, Red Bluff and Socastee are named as target communities, and Socastee has the most repetitive loss properties among them. The plan defines repetitive loss as two or more National Flood Insurance Program claims over $1,000 in ten years.

Mapping is another issue. Under the effective 1999 FEMA maps most flooded Bucksport buildings were in the minimal-risk zone, and in Socastee fewer than 20 percent of damaged buildings (96 of 565) were in the effective Special Flood Hazard Area.

The percentages are in S.C. Code 12-45-180: 3 percent, then 7 percent, then 5 percent. The county page does not list the amounts, so check your notice.

  • Treasurer phone for payments: 843-428-2126.
  • Pay at the Treasurer's Office, by mail, at a night deposit box, online or by phone. Card payments carry a convenience fee.
  • Not receiving a bill does not excuse a late payment, and the notice reflects ownership as of January 1.

Can you pay Horry County tax in installments?

Yes, for real property only, if the application is received before January 15 of the tax year. Escrowed property and personal vehicles are excluded.

The payment is the prior year's tax times 16.67 percent, made in five advance payments due February 15, April 15, June 15, August 15 and October 15. The balance is billed by November 15, and no installment is accepted after October 15.

Applications may be denied for outstanding taxes, a bank escrow account or non-ownership of the property. If you plan to sell mid-year, ask the Treasurer how the plan interacts with your closing.

How do reassessment and the legal residence rate work in Horry County?

Horry County reassesses every four years and implements in the fifth, according to its Assessor. The last was in 2019 and the next was scheduled for tax year 2024, so confirm the current cycle with the office.

Increases from a countywide reappraisal are limited to 15 percent over five years, but the cap does not apply in the year an assessable transfer of interest first becomes taxable. A sale is the usual trigger for that.

  • Legal residence, the 4 percent assessment, must be applied for between January 1 and January 15.
  • Use changes must be reported to the Assessor within six months.
  • The homestead deduction of $50,000 is for owners 65 or older, the blind, the disabled and surviving spouses, and first-time applicants apply in person at the Auditor's Office, 843-915-5051.

How do you appeal an Horry County assessment?

Request a conference in writing within 90 days of the assessment notice. In a year with no notice you can appeal at any time, and an appeal filed before the first penalty date applies to that tax year.

Your letter should include your name, the Map-Block-Parcel number, the value you think is correct and your reasons. The legal basis is S.C. Code 12-60-2510. For agricultural land that changes use, roll-back taxes apply for the year of change and four prior years.

What happens after Horry County taxes become delinquent?

Real property taxes are delinquent on March 17, and notices go out around April 1. Certified notices follow 30 days later, and levy notices are posted on delinquent properties, usually between May and October.

The sale is advertised on three consecutive Thursdays, and the redemption period is 12 months from the sale date. The Delinquent Tax Office is at 1301 Second Avenue, Conway, phone (843) 915-5472, Monday to Friday 8 am to 5 pm. The county said the 2026 sale date and location would appear in a November newspaper ad.

Where is Darlington County and what is its size?

Darlington County sits at about 34°20′N 79°58′W, next to Florence County, with the town of Darlington as the county seat and Hartsville as the largest community. It covers 566.25 square miles, of which 560.59 is land and 5.66 is water.

Neighbors are Florence County to the southeast, Marlboro to the northeast, Chesterfield to the northwest, Lee to the southwest and Kershaw to the west. The county is in the 7th congressional district and the Eastern time zone. The county offices that handle your tax are in the town of Darlington, even if your house is in Hartsville.

What is the history of Darlington County?

The county was established in 1785, by an act passed that March. Its namesake is unknown, though the county may be named for Darlington, England.

The census counted 7,631 people in 1800. The count reached 34,485 in 1880, 50,016 in 1950 and 62,717 in 1980, and was 67,394 in 2000 and 68,681 in 2010.

Has Darlington County grown, and what does the economy look like?

The county has lost population recently: the 2020 census counted 62,905, down 8.4% from 2010, and the 2025 estimate is 62,888. The median age in 2020 was 42.9.

County GDP was $3.3 billion in 2022, or about $52,531 per capita, and unemployment ranged from 2.4% to 4.2% between 2022 and 2024. Manufacturing is the largest employment sector at 18.9%, followed by health care and social assistance at 13.7% and retail trade at 11.6%.

Wikipedia names Coker University, Duke Energy Progress, Sonoco and Walmart among the major employers. Coker is in Hartsville, and Sonoco is among the county's largest employers. Darlington Raceway hosts the NASCAR Southern 500 each year.

Which Darlington County offices handle property tax?

Three offices in the same building at 1 Public Square, Darlington, SC 29532 split the work. The Assessor values property, the Treasurer takes current payments, and the Tax Collector handles delinquent taxes.

  • Treasurer: Room 203, phone 843-398-4160, open 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Monday through Friday except holidays.
  • Tax Collector: Room 207, phone 843-398-4170, same hours.
  • Assessor: Room 309, phone 843-398-4180. County main line is (843) 398-4100.

The Treasurer's page lists several ways to pay current bills: in person, at a drive-thru for current tax bills (8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., near the courthouse), online through the Tax Search, View and Pay portal, or at local banks if you include the tax notice. Banks listed include branches in Darlington, Lamar and Hartsville. When paying by check, write the receipt number on it.

When does Darlington County property tax become delinquent?

Darlington County's Tax Collector says delinquent taxes go to that office on March 17, when a 15% penalty and additional costs are added. This tracks the state penalty statute, which adds 3% after January 15, another 7% by February 2 and another 5% by March 17 (S.C. Code 12-45-180).

On top of the 15%, late costs arrive in three steps.

That totals $120, and all delinquent taxes must be paid before current tax payments are accepted. That rule matters if you plan to pay the current bill and leave an old year open. The office will want the old year cleared first.

How does the Darlington County tax sale work?

Darlington County holds its tax sale in December, starting at 10 a.m. in the gymnasium at Darlington Middle School, 150 Pinedale Drive, Darlington. Call the Tax Collector at 843-398-4170 for the exact date.

The 2026 schedule on the county page is specific. Bidder registration opens November 10, 2026 and must be completed online by December 1, 2026, with a $10 nonrefundable fee. Bidder numbers are issued Saturday, December 5, 2026 at the gymnasium. Real property and mobile homes are advertised in the Darlington News and Press for three consecutive weeks.

  • Delinquent taxes on a parcel must be paid by 5:00 p.m. the day before the sale, and the county says payments cannot be made on the day of the sale.
  • Winning bids must be paid in full by 5:00 p.m. that day by cash, cashier's check or money order.
  • An unpaid winning bid carries a $500 fine.
  • A tax deed is not a warranty deed, and bidders buy at their own risk.

Owners have one year and one day from the sale to redeem, according to the county page. State law states 12 months (S.C. Code 12-51-90), with interest of 3% to 12% of the bid depending on how soon the owner redeems. Confirm the final day with the Tax Collector.

How does reassessment and the 4% rate work in Darlington County?

The Darlington County Assessor inspects property on a five-year cycle under a revaluation plan approved by the SC Department of Revenue. Inspections can come sooner for new construction, renovation or an appraisal review.

Owner-occupied homes qualify for a 4% assessment ratio, and non-owner-occupied property is assessed at 6%. Apply by filing a legal residence application, ideally once the deed or bond for title is recorded and you move in. You may file any time before the first penalty date, January 15. The Assessor warns that an owner who loses eligibility and does not report it within six months faces a penalty of 100% of the tax paid plus 0.5% interest per month, at least $30 and no more than that year's tax.

The owner on December 31 is named on the tax bill, and a buyer becomes responsible once a sale is final after that date. State law gives 90 days from the mailed notice to object in writing to the Assessor (S.C. Code 12-60-2510). The county page links to a protest of valuation form and a Board of Assessment and Appeals but gives no deadlines, so call 843-398-4180.

The Assessor's page says both that it processes state exemptions and that it does not grant real property exemptions. Ask the office which applies to your situation.

What should a Darlington County seller with back taxes do?

A Darlington County seller with unpaid tax can still sell, and the title company normally pays the balance from the sale proceeds. Get a written payoff from the Tax Collector, since the $20, $40 and $60 cost steps mean the figure changes over the year.

Do not wait for the tax sale calendar. The county advertises properties for three weeks, and the last chance to pay a parcel's delinquent taxes is 5:00 p.m. the day before the sale. If a sale has already happened, the redemption period still lets you pay, and the county says successful bidders wait at least a year and a day before gaining a vested interest.

Where is Aiken County and what is in it?

The county seat and largest community is the city of Aiken. Other cities are New Ellenton and North Augusta, which is partly in Edgefield County. Aiken County was organized in 1871 from parts of Barnwell, Edgefield, Lexington and Orangeburg counties. It was named for William Aiken, the first president of the South Carolina Railroad Company.

In the late 19th century the county became a winter refuge for wealthy Northerners, who built large houses, and it remains known for horse training because the winters are mild. In the 1950s the Savannah River Site was built, which required acquiring the town of Ellenton. Its residents and businesses moved about eight miles north to New Ellenton and about five miles south to Jackson.

Newberry County was formed in 1785 from the Ninety-Six District, and the town of Newberry was founded in 1789 as its seat. The origin of the name is unknown, though one theory ties it to Quaker settlers and Newbury Park in London.

Cotton was the main crop before the Civil War. The railroad reached the county in the early 1850s, the Lutheran Church founded Newberry College in 1856, and the first cotton mills opened in the 1880s.

Fighting in the Revolution came before the county existed: Williams' Plantation on December 31, 1780, Mud Lick on March 2, 1781, and Bush River in May 1781. The population has risen from 29,416 in 1960 to 37,719 in 2020, a slow climb compared with the Columbia suburbs to the southeast.

Laurens County by the numbers

Where is Laurens County and how is it laid out?

Laurens County sits in the Upstate of South Carolina and belongs to the Greenville-Anderson-Greer metropolitan area. It covers 722.93 square miles, of which 712.87 are land, and part of the Sumter National Forest lies inside its borders.

The county seat and largest community is the city of Laurens. Clinton is the other main town, and the county also includes Cross Hill, Gray Court, Waterloo, Barksdale, Hickory Tavern, Madden and Owings. Fountain Inn is mostly in Greenville County, Ware Shoals is mostly in Greenwood County, and Kinards straddles the line with Newberry County.

Seven counties touch Laurens: Spartanburg, Union, Newberry, Greenwood, Abbeville, Anderson and Greenville. The 2020 census counted 67,539 residents, and about 64 percent of the population lived in rural areas. For a seller, that rural share matters because a farmhouse outside Gray Court and a bungalow in the city of Laurens are taxed by the same county offices but attract very different buyers.

What shaped Laurens County, and what does it mean for older houses?

The county was formed on March 12, 1785, and was named for Henry Laurens, a president of the Continental Congress. It was one of nine modern counties carved from the old Ninety-Six District.

The Battle of Musgrove Mill, an American Revolution engagement, took place here. Andrew Johnson, later the 17th president, worked as a tailor in the town of Laurens in the 1820s. Presbyterian College in Clinton was founded in 1880.

That long settlement history means the county has plenty of older homes, including mill-era houses and farm property that may have passed through several generations. Inherited houses often arrive with unpaid tax bills, unclear titles or no one living in them, and each of those problems affects how quickly a sale can close.

What do people in Laurens County do for work?

Manufacturing is the largest employer group in Laurens County. In the third quarter of 2023 it accounted for 7,641 of 20,836 jobs, or 36.7 percent, at an average annual wage of $57,772.

The same data shows health care and social assistance at 9.8 percent of jobs, retail at 8.5 percent and educational services at 8.4 percent. As of April 2024 the larger employers named for the county were CeramTec, National Healthcare, Presbyterian College, Shaw Industries, Sterilite and Walmart. The county's 2022 gross domestic product was $2.7 billion.

A plant closing or a shift change can move the local housing market quickly in a county this dependent on factories. Sellers who need to move on a deadline often find that waiting for a retail buyer to secure a mortgage costs them more in carrying costs, including tax, than the sale price difference they hoped to gain.

Which offices handle Laurens County property tax?

Four county offices share the work, and each answers a different question. The county's own property tax page lists them this way:

  • Assessor, 864-984-6546: sets appraisal values for real property and handles legal residence questions.
  • Auditor, 864-984-2535: calculates the tax and handles exemption paperwork.
  • Treasurer: collects payments but does not set amounts or keep owner records.
  • Tax Collector, 864-984-4742: takes over accounts that are still unpaid after the March deadline.

The Treasurer does not keep owner records, so a bill mailed to an old address can simply go astray. If you inherited a house or bought one recently, tell the Assessor that your address changed. The county page also says the County Council, the school board and the municipal councils decide how much revenue they need, which means a rate increase comes from them and not from the Treasurer.

When are Laurens County property taxes due, and when do they become delinquent?

Laurens County property tax is due by January 15 without penalty. When that day falls on a weekend or holiday, payment is accepted until 5:00 p.m. on the next business day, and bills must be mailed at least 30 days before the due date.

After March 16, or the next business day if that date lands on a weekend or holiday, unpaid accounts go to the Tax Collector. State law sets the penalty steps that build up before that point.

DateWhat happens
January 15Last day to pay without penalty (county page)
After January 153 percent penalty under S.C. Code 12-45-180
February 2Further 7 percent penalty under the same section
March 17Further 5 percent penalty, and the Treasurer may issue a tax execution
After March 16Account turned over to the Tax Collector (county page)

The state penalties stack, so an account that runs all the way to March has grown by 15 percent before any collection costs are added.

How do you challenge an assessment in Laurens County?

A Laurens County owner objects in writing to the Assessor, and under state law the deadline is 90 days after the Assessor mails the assessment notice. The objection can cover fair market value, special use value or the assessment ratio.

State law requires a written notice only when the Assessor raises a value by $1,000 or more or assesses a property for the first time. If no notice was sent, the taxpayer can appeal in writing at any time. An appeal filed before the first penalty date applies to the current tax year, and one filed on or after that date applies to the following year.

The Laurens County pages we opened do not explain the local appeal board or hearing schedule, so ask the Assessor at 864-984-6546 for the form and the next step. Do not skip paying while an appeal is open without confirming with the office what balance is protected.

What is the difference between the 4 percent and 6 percent rates?

South Carolina assesses a legal residence at 4 percent of fair market value and other real property at 6 percent. A house that fails the legal residence test is therefore assessed at one and a half times the ratio of an owner-occupied home.

Under S.C. Code 12-43-220, the rules for the 4 percent ratio include:

  • The owner holds the property and lives in it as a legal residence.
  • The owner certifies under penalty of perjury that no one in the household claims the ratio on another home.
  • The residence is not rented for more than 72 days in a calendar year.
  • After a sale, the new owner must apply, and the former owner must tell the assessor within six months.

The application has to be filed before the first penalty date of the year the owner first claims the ratio. A buyer who closes in the fall and misses that date pays at the 6 percent ratio for the year, which is one reason buyers in Laurens County often ask sellers to leave records tidy.

Laurens County also offers a homestead exemption that excludes the first $50,000 of a legal residence's fair market value for owners who are 65 or older, certified totally and permanently disabled, or legally blind. Details go through the Auditor.

What happens when taxes on a Laurens County house go unpaid?

Unpaid Laurens County taxes lead to a delinquent tax sale run by the Delinquent Tax Collector's office under Chapter 51 of Title 12 of the state code. The owner keeps the right to redeem the property for twelve months after the sale.

The county's sale page, which described the December 6, 2023 sale, says the list is advertised in the Laurens County Advertiser and the Clinton Chronicle, that the opening bid is placed for the Forfeited Land Commission, and that bidders must register ahead and attend in person. A tax deed is issued within 45 days after the redemption period ends. Sale dates change every year, so call the office at 864-984-4742 for the current one.

Under S.C. Code 12-51-90, redemption interest is a share of the bid amount that rises by quarter:

Months after saleInterest on bid amount
1 to 33 percent
4 to 66 percent
7 to 99 percent
10 to 1212 percent

The defaulting owner, a grantee of the owner, or a mortgage or judgment creditor may redeem.

How are taxes handled when a Laurens County house is sold?

Taxes for the year are normally paid at the closing table, and the title company pays any unpaid balance from the seller's proceeds. Before a closing, ask the Treasurer or Tax Collector for the exact payoff, because penalties change on fixed dates.

Sellers in Laurens County often face a few predictable problems:

  • A tax bill sent to a deceased parent's address that nobody opened.
  • Penalties that started on January 16 and kept growing into March.
  • A legal residence ratio that lapsed after a move, leaving the 6 percent ratio in place.
  • An older house needing repairs that a mortgage lender would not accept.

Owners with unpaid tax or repairs sometimes choose an as-is cash sale. The tax is paid from proceeds at closing, so you do not need cash up front to clear it.

Call the Tax Collector at 864-984-4742. The county says delinquent accounts are turned over to that office after March 16.

Can I appeal my Laurens County assessment?

Yes. Send a written objection to the Assessor within 90 days of the date the assessment notice was mailed. Call 864-984-6546 for the form.

Does the county tax homes at 4 percent?

Only a legal residence qualifies for the 4 percent ratio. Other real property is assessed at 6 percent, and renting the home more than 72 days a year can cost you the lower ratio.

How long can I redeem a Laurens County house after a tax sale?

State law gives twelve months after the sale date, with interest that rises from 3 to 12 percent of the bid depending on the quarter you redeem.

Can I sell a house in Laurens County that owes back taxes?

Yes. The balance is paid from the sale proceeds at closing, as long as the sale price covers what is owed. Ask the Tax Collector for a current payoff figure first.

Where is Oconee County and what does it include?

Oconee County is the westernmost county in South Carolina and borders both Georgia and North Carolina. It measures 673.57 square miles in total, of which 626.56 are land and 47.01 are water, so about 7% of the county sits under lakes.

Walhalla is the county seat and Seneca is the largest community.   • Hart, Franklin, Stephens, Habersham and Rabun counties in Georgia sit to the south and west.

A house on a county road near Mountain Rest and a home on Lake Keowee are billed through the same Oconee County offices.

How did Oconee County get its name and shape?

Oconee County was formed in 1868 when the state legislature divided Pickens County. The name comes from the Cherokee word Ae-quo-nee, usually given as "land beside the water."

That description fits the county today. Lake Hartwell, Lake Keowee and Lake Jocassee cover large areas, and the state parks and preserves around them include Devils Fork State Park, Oconee State Park and Stumphouse Mountain Heritage Preserve.

For a seller, lakefront and hillside parcels can raise questions about access and shoreline rules that a town lot does not, so ask the county offices what applies to your address.

Manufacturing is the largest employment sector in Oconee County, at 24.8% of jobs in the third quarter of 2023, followed by retail trade at 16.0%. County output in 2022 was about $4.5 billion, or roughly $56,008 per person.

Employers named in the county's profile include Apex Tool Group, BorgWarner, Duke Energy, Prisma Health, Sandvik, Schneider Electric and Walmart. The Oconee Nuclear Station is also among the county's listed landmarks.

When are Oconee County property taxes due, and how do you pay them?

Oconee County property taxes (other than vehicles) are due by January 15, after a notice that arrives in the fall. For 2026 the county expected online notices by October 10 and printed notices in the mail by October 20, and it said those dates could change.

State law puts the payable window between September 30 and January 15 (S.C. Code 12-45-70). If the due date falls on a weekend or a county holiday it moves to the next business day, and a mailed payment counts if it is postmarked by the deadline.

The Auditor's Office is at 415 S. Pine St. in Walhalla, open Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. The county lists 864-638-4162 for paying taxes and 864-638-4158 for tax notices and other questions.

What penalties apply if the bill is not paid in Oconee County?

Under S.C. Code 12-45-180, a 3% penalty is added after January 15, another 7% if the bill is still open before February 2, and another 5% before March 17. After March 17 the treasurer sends an execution to the officer who collects delinquent taxes.

One sentence in that section matters at closing. If title moved during the tax year, the tax notice went to the previous owner, and the new owner never got a timely notice, penalties are waived. The seller should still pass along any notice that arrives after the deed records.

Oconee County runs its own tax sale through the Delinquent Tax Office, which you can reach at 864-638-4147. The county advertises each sale in the Seneca Journal Tribune for three weeks and only pre-registered bidders may bid.

What happens in an Oconee County tax sale, and can the owner get the house back?

A tax sale in Oconee County is an auction of the property to the highest bidder, and the owner has one year from the sale date to redeem. The sale is a collection method under S.C. Code Title 12, Chapter 51.

The owner, a grantee from the owner, or a mortgage or judgment creditor may redeem by paying the taxes, assessments, penalties and costs plus interest on the full bid. That interest rises by quarter.

  • Months 1 to 3: 3%
  • Months 4 to 6: 6%
  • Months 7 to 9: 9%
  • Final three months: 12%

A winning bidder who fails to pay by 4:00 p.m. on sale day is liable for $500 per parcel. Property nobody bids on goes to the county's Forfeited Land Commission for the amount owed. If the year passes with no redemption, the property is conveyed by quitclaim deed, generally within 30 days.

How do you appeal an Oconee County assessment?

You start with a written objection to the Assessor within 90 days of the date on the assessment notice. If no notice was sent that year, the county says you may object until January 15 of the following year.

  1. Send your name, address and phone, a description of the property, your reasons, your estimate of fair market value and supporting documents.
  2. The Assessor reviews the file, sets a conference, may inspect the property and answers in writing.
  3. Within 30 days of that answer, give written notice to appeal to the Board of Assessment Appeals at 415 S. Pine St., Walhalla.
  4. Within 30 days of the Board's decision, ask the Administrative Law Judge Division in Columbia for a contested case hearing.

If the appeal will probably not be settled by December 31, you must pay 80% of the tax on your proposed assessment, and you can ask in writing for a 100% bill. The result can be no change, a lower value or a higher one, so weigh that risk. The Assessor can be reached at 864-638-4150.

What does the 4% legal residence rate mean when you sell in Oconee County?

The 4% rate applies to the owner's legal residence and up to five contiguous acres, and other real property is assessed at 6% (S.C. Code 12-43-220). Oconee County says the school tax credit on owner-occupied homes is automatic once the 4% ratio is granted.

The home cannot be rented for more than 72 days in a calendar year. If an owner loses eligibility and does not tell the Assessor within six months, the statute allows a penalty of 100% of the tax paid plus interest at 0.5% per month, with a $30 minimum.

A seller who moved out and rented the house for a year should expect the 6% rate to apply, and a cash buyer will price the carrying cost accordingly. To check which rate your parcel has, call the Assessor at 864-638-4150.

What is the cost of transferring a deed in Oconee County?

South Carolina charges a deed recording fee of $1.85 for each $500 of value, made up of $1.30 for the state and $0.55 for the county (S.C. Code 12-24-10 and 12-24-90). A deed given to a lender in lieu of foreclosure, or a foreclosure deed, is on the exempt list in 12-24-40.

Property valuation is also tied to the sale. Under the five-year appraisal rule in 12-43-217, the county revalues every fifth year, and the Assessor must send a notice when value changes by $1,000 or more. Oconee County's own pages do not state its next reassessment year, so ask the Assessor.

Taxes do not disappear at closing. They are normally prorated between the parties, and any bill open in January should be paid from the proceeds so a new owner never inherits a penalty.

What do Oconee County sellers usually run into?

Sellers in Oconee County most often face an inherited house with years of unpaid tax, a lake or hillside property that needs repairs before a bank will lend, or a rental that has turned into a burden. Each has a tax angle.

  • Heirs selling a family house should ask the Assessor whether the 4% rate is still attached.
  • An owner who is behind should call the Delinquent Tax Office at 864-638-4147 before the sale is advertised.
  • A cash buyer does not depend on a lender's appraisal to close.

By January 15, with notices going out in the fall. The county expected online notices by October 10 and mailed notices by October 20 for 2026.

How long do you have to appeal an Oconee County assessment?

You have 90 days from the date on the assessment notice to object in writing to the Assessor. If no notice was issued, the county allows an appeal until January 15 of the following year.

Can I redeem my house after an Oconee County tax sale?

Yes, for one year from the sale date, by paying the taxes, costs and penalties plus interest of 3%, 6%, 9% or 12% depending on the quarter. After that the property is conveyed to the buyer.

Who do I call about Oconee County property taxes?

Call 864-638-4162 to pay, 864-638-4158 for tax notices, the Assessor at 864-638-4150 for values, or Delinquent Tax at 864-638-4147. All offices are at 415 S. Pine St., Walhalla.

How do you appeal a Pickens County assessment?

In a year with a Notice of Valuation, you must object in writing within 90 days after the Assessor mails it. In a year with no notice, you file before the first penalty date, and a filing before that date applies to the current tax year while a later one applies to the next.

  1. Informal review: a licensed appraiser looks at every timely appeal.
  2. Notice of Decision: the Assessor mails the result.
  3. Pickens County Board of Assessment Appeals: file written notice with the Assessor within 30 days of the decision date.
  4. Administrative Law Judge Division: appeal within 30 days of the Board's written decision.

Appeals cannot be faxed and must go to the Assessor, not another county office. An agent needs a signed authorization or power of attorney from the owner. The county warns that a missed deadline or a wrong filing can get an appeal dismissed. The Assessor's number is (864) 898-5872.

When does a sale trigger a reassessment in Pickens County?

A recorded deed can trigger a reassessment, even when no money changes hands. The Assessor calls this an Assessable Transfer of Interest, and it raises the value to fair market value as of December 31 of the year of transfer.

The last countywide reassessment took effect December 31, 2018, and appeared on 2019 notices. State law calls for a reappraisal every fifth year, and the Assessor must send a Notice of Valuation when value rises by $1,000 or more (S.C. Code 12-43-217). The Assessor's FAQ does not state the next reassessment year, so ask the office.

The owner on December 31 is liable for that year's tax, and the lien follows the property. The bill therefore follows the property, so a closing should settle it.

How does the 4% legal residence rate affect a Pickens County sale?

An owner-occupied primary home is assessed at 4%, and anything not owner-occupied is assessed at 6%. The application goes to the Assessor after the deed records and you move in, due before the first penalty date.

A transfer into a trust requires a new application. The 4% rate is removed for trust transfers unless the income beneficiary lives in the home as a primary residence and the trustee certifies it. If eligibility ends and you do not tell the Assessor within six months, the penalty can reach 100% of the tax paid plus interest.

Estate and rental sellers should check the status first. A rate that changed from 4% to 6% raises the bill the buyer will see.

Statewide, the deed recording fee is $1.85 per $500 of value, split $1.30 state and $0.55 county, and a deed in lieu of foreclosure is exempt (S.C. Code 12-24-10 and 12-24-40).

What do Pickens County sellers usually deal with?

Sellers here often hold an inherited house in Easley or Pickens, a rental near Clemson that has aged, or a mountain property that is hard to maintain. Several offices matter.

  • Treasurer, (864) 898-5883, for the current bill.
  • Auditor, (864) 898-5895, for personal property and homestead exemption questions.
  • Assessor, (864) 898-5872, for the rate and value.
  • Delinquent Tax, (864) 898-5890, for anything past March 16.

January 15 is the last day to pay without penalty. The Treasurer collects current taxes from October 1 to March 16.

It is at 222 McDaniel Avenue, B-6, Pickens, SC 29671, open 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Monday to Friday. The phone number is (864) 898-5883.

File a written objection with the Assessor within 90 days of the Notice of Valuation. If you disagree with the decision, you can go to the County Board of Assessment Appeals within 30 days, then to the Administrative Law Judge Division.

Does selling a house reassess it in Pickens County?

Yes, a recorded deed can trigger an Assessable Transfer of Interest. The value is raised to fair market value as of December 31 of the transfer year.

Who do I call about delinquent taxes in Pickens County?

Call the Delinquent Tax Office at (864) 898-5890. It is located at 222 McDaniel Avenue, B-15, Pickens.

Yes. The title company pays the tax from the proceeds at closing, and Cash Home Buyers can buy the house as it is.

Colleton County by the numbers

Where is Colleton County and how big is it?

Colleton County is in the South Carolina Lowcountry, and Walterboro is the county seat and largest community. It covers 1,133.28 square miles, of which 1,056.50 is land and 76.78 is water.

That makes it the fifth-largest county in the state by land area and the fourth by total area. Orangeburg lies to the north, Dorchester to the northeast, Charleston to the east, Beaufort to the south, Hampton and Allendale to the west and Bamberg to the northwest.

Rivers and wetlands shape the map. The Edisto, Salkehatchie and Ashepoo rivers run through the county, along with the Intracoastal Waterway. Protected land includes Bear Island and Donnelley Wildlife Management Areas and Colleton State Park.

What is the history of Colleton County?

The county was created in 1682 as one of three original proprietary counties of the colony, and it is named for Sir John Colleton, one of the eight Lords Proprietor. In 1706 it was divided into St. Bartholomew and St. Paul parishes, where planters developed rice and indigo plantations worked by enslaved Africans.

The present county was created in 1800 from the western half of Charleston District and reorganized as a county in 1868. It then lost ground several times: Dorchester County split off in 1897, eastern land went to Charleston County in 1911, and small areas went to Bamberg County in 1919 and 1920. Edisto Beach was annexed into Colleton from Charleston County in 1975.

How many people live in Colleton County and what do they do for work?

The 2020 census counted 38,604 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 39,382. Population peaked at 41,916 in 1860 in the historical table, fell to a low of 25,821 in 1930, and has hovered near 38,000 to 39,000 since 2000.

County GDP was about $1.1 billion in 2022, and unemployment ranged between 2.6% and 4.3% from 2022 to 2024. The largest employment sectors are retail trade (17.1%), health care and social assistance (15.5%), and accommodation and food services (14.1%). Major employers named on the county's Wikipedia page are Colleton County School District, Cracker Barrel, Food Lion and Walmart.

Who handles property tax in Colleton County?

The Treasurer's page also says the Assessor keeps land and building records, while the Auditor keeps personal property and vehicle records, so an address error needs to be reported to the right office.

When are Colleton County property taxes due and what are the penalties?

The Colleton pages we opened did not list a real property due date or penalty schedule, so we rely on state law here. Under S.C. Code 12-45-180, a 3% penalty applies if tax is unpaid by January 16 (or 30 days after notices are mailed, if later), another 7% by February 2, and another 5% by March 17.

If the amount is still unpaid on March 17, the county treasurer issues an execution to the officer who collects delinquent taxes. A U.S. postmark decides whether a mailed payment was on time.

The Assessor's page adds a date that matters at sale time: the owner of record on December 31 is the name on the tax bill, and a sale that closes after that date makes the new owner responsible for the following tax. Ask the Treasurer for the exact billing and payoff figure.

How does a Colleton County tax sale work?

Colleton County auctions properties with unpaid tax once a year, and the 2026 sale is set for Friday, December 11, 2026 at the Colleton Civic Center, 494 Hampton St., Walterboro. Registration begins at 9:00 a.m. and bidding at 10:00 a.m.

Properties are sold alphabetically by the taxpayer's last name. The opening bid covers delinquent taxes for tax year 2025 and prior years, plus the 2026 taxes. A winning bidder who fails to pay faces a $500 fine per bid. The county says the buyer gets title without warranty, and a tax sale does not erase existing liens.

An owner has 12 months to redeem under S.C. Code 12-51-90. The defaulting taxpayer, a grantee from the owner, or a mortgage or judgment creditor may redeem. Interest is based on the bid amount.

The county's page puts the redemption window at 12 months, and also describes it as up to one year and one day. Call the Delinquent Tax Office to confirm the exact last day for any parcel.

How does the Colleton County reassessment and 4% rate work?

South Carolina counties must reassess every five years on a staggered schedule, and the Colleton Assessor must notify you of any change in value or classification of $1,000 or more. Increases in market value are capped at 15% within each five-year cycle, but new construction, major additions and renovation are added at current market value.

Owner-occupied primary residences can get the 4% assessment ratio, and everything else is assessed at 6%. You must apply, and the application can be filed any time before the first penalty date of January 15. The Assessor says to file once your deed or bond for title is recorded and you move in. Changes in use or ownership must be reported within six months, and a new owner needs a new application.

  • The first step in an appeal after a notice is a written objection to the Assessor within 90 days of the dated notice.
  • The Assessor does a field review and answers in writing.
  • You then have 30 days to file a written appeal with the Colleton County Board of Assessment Appeals.
  • With no notice that year, an appeal filed before the first penalty date applies to that year, and one filed later applies to the next.

The Assessor makes clear that worry over a higher tax bill is not a basis for appeal, because millage is set each year by the taxing authorities.

What should a Colleton County seller with unpaid tax know?

A seller can still close with back taxes owing, and the title company normally pays them from the proceeds. Get a payoff from the Treasurer or Delinquent Tax Office in writing, because the penalty steps and the year-end tax sale both move the number.

Owners aged 65 or older, totally and permanently disabled or legally blind may qualify for the homestead exemption on the first $50,000 of fair market value of a legal residence, according to the Treasurer's page. Surviving spouses may also qualify, per the Assessor's reassessment guide. Contact the Auditor's Office for the requirements.

If a house has been vacant, rented out or inherited, check that the 4% application is on file under the right owner before you list, since a missing application means the 6% rate.

Twelve months from the sale under state law, with interest of 3%, 6%, 9% or 12% depending on the quarter. The county page also describes it as one year and one day, so confirm the exact date with the Delinquent Tax Office.

File a legal residence application with the Assessor before January 15. Owner-occupied primary homes qualify, and everything else is assessed at 6%. You must report changes in use within six months.

Orangeburg County by the numbers

Where is Orangeburg County and how big is it?

Orangeburg County sits in the Midlands region of South Carolina and covers 1,127.89 square miles, with 1,106.38 of that land.

The city of Orangeburg is both the county seat and the largest community. The county is named for William IV, Prince of Orange, and Wikipedia traces it to the Orangeburg Judicial District of 1769.

  • Calhoun, Clarendon and Lexington counties lie to the north.
  • Dorchester, Berkeley, Colleton and Bamberg counties lie to the south and southeast.
  • Aiken and Barnwell counties are to the west.

The 2020 Census counted 84,223 residents. A seller in the city and one on a farm road in the south are billed by the same county but face very different buyer pools.

What shapes the Orangeburg County economy?

Orangeburg County combines farming, factories and two universities. Manufacturing is the largest employment sector at 17.3%, followed by retail trade at 14.6%, and 2022 output was about $3.4 billion, or $40,510 per person.

Major crops are cotton, soybeans, corn, turf grass and watermelons. Employers named for the county include South Carolina State University, Claflin University, Orangeburg-Calhoun Technical College, the Medical University of South Carolina, Husqvarna Group, Okonite, Love's, GPM Investments and Walmart.

South Carolina State University is the state's only public four-year historically Black university, and Claflin University is the oldest HBCU in the state.

When are Orangeburg County property taxes due?

Real property taxes in Orangeburg County are due January 15, and unpaid taxes become delinquent on March 17. Motor vehicles follow a separate schedule.

State law sets the penalty steps: 3% after the January 15 deadline, 7% more before February 2 and 5% more before March 17 (S.C. Code 12-45-180). Mailed payments count by postmark.

  • The Assessor's office is at 1437 Amelia Street, Orangeburg, SC 29115.
  • The mailing address is P.O. Box 9000, Attn: County Assessor, Orangeburg, SC 29116-9000.
  • The Assessor's phone is 803-533-6220.
  • The Delinquent Tax Collector's counter hours are Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

For payment details, check with the Treasurer, since the pages we opened list the Assessor and Delinquent Tax offices rather than a Treasurer phone number.

How often does Orangeburg County reassess property?

The county reappraises on a five-year schedule, which state law requires (S.C. Code 12-43-217). Orangeburg County's own FAQ says values may rise or fall with the market, the property's condition and other factors.

It also explains that an assessment notice is not a tax bill, and that notices go out mainly the year after a value change, a discovered error, a transfer or a countywide reassessment. The FAQ does not name the next reassessment year, so ask the office.

A sale can start its own reassessment. The county calls it an Assessable Transfer of Interest, and the effective appraisal date is December 31 of the year the deed was conveyed. The 15% cap on yearly increases was removed for these transfers after the 2006 tax year.

Plan for the buyer's bill to be based on the sale, not on your old value.

How do you appeal an Orangeburg County assessment?

Submit a written appeal within 90 days of the assessment notice, and if no notice was issued, by January 15, the first penalty date on the tax notice. The county says the appeal must be in writing.

The county's FAQ makes one point clearly: an appeal does not stop payment, and penalties still apply if the bill is not paid by January 15. A refund is issued only when an adjustment warrants one.

  • Agricultural classification applications (timberland or cropland) are due January 15, including for people who inherited property during the tax year.
  • If farmland changes to another use, rollback taxes can reach back three years.
  • Appeals can be directed to the Assessor at 803-533-6220.

An inheritor with farmland should file the agricultural application on time, because January 15 is the county's stated deadline.

What does the 4% legal residence rate mean here?

Taxpayers who own and occupy their home can apply for the 4% legal residence rate, and the application is on the Assessor's website. State law assesses all other real property at 6% (S.C. Code 12-43-220).

The 4% rate covers the home and up to five contiguous acres, and the owner cannot rent the house for more than 72 days in a calendar year. An owner who loses eligibility and does not report it within six months can face a penalty equal to the tax paid, plus interest at 0.5% per month, with a $30 floor.

The county page we read does not give a deadline for the application, so call before you list the house.

What happens in an Orangeburg County tax sale?

If taxes stay unpaid, the Delinquent Tax Collector can sell the property, and the owner has one year from the sale date to redeem. Real estate is advertised for three weeks before the sale and mobile homes for the final two weeks.

The owner, a grantee from the owner, or a mortgage or judgment creditor may redeem. The cost is all taxes, costs, assessments and penalties plus interest on the whole bid, rising by quarter.

  1. Months 1 to 3: 3%
  2. Months 4 to 6: 6%
  3. Months 7 to 9: 9%
  4. Months 10 to 12: 12%

Interest cannot exceed the bid submitted for the forfeited land commission. A mobile home owner redeeming also pays the bidder rent, capped at one-twelfth of the last completed year's taxes with a $10 monthly minimum. During the year the bidder has no ownership rights and cannot enter the property. After the year, the Tax Collector issues a tax deed as soon as possible.

What does a deed transfer cost in Orangeburg County?

The deed recording fee is $1.85 for every $500 of value, of which $1.30 goes to the state and $0.55 to the county (S.C. Code 12-24-10 and 12-24-90). A deed in lieu of foreclosure and a foreclosure deed to the lender are exempt under 12-24-40.

The fee is based on the value of the property sold, so it scales with the sale price. Ask the closing attorney or title company for the exact figure.

What do Orangeburg County sellers usually face?

Sellers in Orangeburg County often hold an inherited house, farmland with a classification to protect, or an older home that needs work. Each has a tax deadline to watch.

  • Check the January 15 date for appeals and agricultural applications.
  • Ask for a payoff figure before March 17, when taxes become delinquent.
  • Confirm whether the 4% rate was in place for the last owner.

Cash Home Buyers buys houses as they are, so a seller who cannot afford repairs can still ask for an offer. Gather the county numbers first and you will know what the proceeds look like.

More questions about Orangeburg County, SC Property Tax Guide

When are Orangeburg County SC property taxes due?

January 15 is the due date for real property tax. Unpaid taxes become delinquent on March 17.

How long do I have to appeal an Orangeburg County assessment?

You have 90 days from the assessment notice. If no notice was sent, the deadline is January 15, the first penalty date on the tax notice.

Does an appeal stop me from paying Orangeburg County taxes?

No. The county says an appeal does not stop payment or prevent penalties if the bill is not paid by January 15.

How long is the redemption period after an Orangeburg County tax sale?

One year from the sale date. Redemption interest runs 3%, 6%, 9% or 12% depending on the quarter.

How often does Orangeburg County reassess?

The county reappraises on a five-year schedule required by state law. A sale can also trigger an individual reassessment effective December 31 of the conveyance year.

Can I sell my Orangeburg County house with back taxes?

Yes. The taxes are settled from the proceeds at closing, and Cash Home Buyers can buy the house in its current condition.
